title: The gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is widening
titleZh: The gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is widening
author: albertzeyer
relevanceReason: 命中 6 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

comments.author: athrowaway3z
comments.textRawHtml:
I agree with the disconnect between the professionals, but i have yet to see anything that makes me believe that there is a class of 5000 internal people who are that much further than the top users are.

The internal models are more eager, and there is the scale difference of being able to spin up 10.000 vs 10, but to get something valuable out requires skill.

Agents that produce good results 90% of the time vs 93% of the time are not enough of a difference. Multiplied too many times, that error rate is too high for scale to become "magic".

Finding proofs is one of the exceptions.

Just look at the codex/claude harness. They regularly lag behind 'external' users.

children.author: jrowen
children.textRawHtml:
I feel like you're taking it somewhat personally as a statement on ability or intelligence levels. It's really just about the scale difference and the access to that infrastructure. That is what enables that class to look at and think about problems differently.

Having 10,000 (or more) agents working for months on a problem is categorically different from the type of usage most people are familiar with. The complexity explodes to a point that requires the "archaeology" he mentions for people to even try to understand what's going on.

This is the key insight. Those capabilities are currently limited to frontier labs and literally cost them millions of dollars to achieve. But as we well know, computing costs and algorithms are optimized rapidly and soon those capabilities will be more widespread. We are at an inflection point where we can design systems that are able to go and do things that we don't fully understand, and they will handily outpace our forensic bandwidth.

children.author: DenisM
children.textRawHtml:
You might be thinking along the lines of the O-ring theory. Indeed long supply chains accumulate errors exponentially.

However the origins of theory explored the outcome of disastrous and irreparable outcome of space shuttle exploding, lives lost, and billion of dollars destroyed.

When LLM goes off the rails the cost is much lower, and retry is on the table. In fact our core competency shifted from writing code to creating environment where agents can retry cheaply and course correct based on feedback.

A modest increase in the number of turns it takes to reach decorehenve could make a difference between Decoherence and reaching the a grounded checkpoint.

children.author: zamadatix
children.textRawHtml:
Which is precisely what I'm responding about above. 93% actually collapses much slower than 90% since the rate of reduction is based on that of all of the previous rounds, not just the current chance. E.g., this is the difference between 14 rounds before an expected failure instead of 10. An extra 4 rounds deep at the same error rate is a big step forward despite a small change in the base percentages. Add just few more percentage points again and you've more than doubled the depth.

I.e. it's precisely when you look at these chained that the difference is actually very large. It's really only the 1st turn or two of prompts where the difference seems negligable.

children.author: jdiff
children.textRawHtml:
How are you running that math and what are you consider to be "expected failure"? If even 30% of your runs go into the garbage, that sounds horrifically unreliable, and both 7 and 10% failure rates hit those margins in less than 5 iterations.

Not to mention that the deeper your iterations, the more money burned on garbage before you realize that data in turned to garbage out turned to garbage in somewhere in the chain.
